name: Pawn structure
mnemonic: Pawns are the skeleton; pieces are the muscles. Attack a chain at its base.
summary: Pawns can't move backwards, so their placement decides which squares are strong, which are weak, and where each side should play.
points: A pawn chain (here d4–e5) is strongest at its head and weakest at its base: Black attacks d4 with ...c5 and the head with ...f6.
Pawns point to where you should attack: White's chain points to the kingside, Black's to the queenside.
Isolated, doubled and backward pawns are long-term weaknesses; passed pawns are long-term strengths.

name: Weak squares
mnemonic: A hole is a square no pawn can ever guard again.
summary: A square that can no longer be defended by a pawn is a permanent home for enemy pieces.
points: After ...e5 in the Najdorf, d5 can't be covered by a black pawn any more — it's a hole.
Black compensates by controlling d5 with pieces (...Be6, ...Nbd7–b6) or by forcing the ...d5 break.
Every pawn move creates a potential weakness behind it — move pawns with a purpose.

name: Outposts
mnemonic: A knight on an outpost is like a tooth in the opponent's jaw.
summary: An outpost is a square in enemy territory, protected by your pawn, that no enemy pawn can attack. Knights love them.
points: The d5-knight is supported by two pawns and can never be chased by a black pawn (no c- or e-pawn can reach c6/e6).
From d5 it hits c7, e7, b6 and f6 — it controls Black's whole position.
The only way to remove it is to trade a piece for it; often Black has no suitable piece.

name: Open files
mnemonic: Rooks belong on open files — and then on the 7th rank.
summary: A file with no pawns is a highway for rooks. Controlling it lets your rooks invade the enemy position.
points: Doubling rooks (here on d1 and d2) wins control of the file — a single rook can be challenged.
The goal is to invade: a rook on the 7th rank attacks pawns and confines the king.
Contest open files early; once the enemy doubles, you may never get in.

name: Piece activity
summary: A piece is only as good as the squares it controls. Active pieces win games even without extra material.
points: Material is equal, but White's rook on the 7th and centralised knight dominate Black's undeveloped rook and knight.
Ask every move: which piece is doing least? Move that one.
Trade your bad pieces; keep your good ones.

name: King safety
mnemonic: Pawns in front of your king are walls — every pawn move is a brick removed.
summary: Castle early, keep the pawn shield intact, and don't open lines towards your own king.
points: ...h6 and ...g5 gained time against the bishop but tore holes on f5 and h5 next to Black's king.
White's knight heads for f5 via h4; the queen can follow to h5.
Count attackers vs defenders around the king; if the attackers outnumber defenders, a sacrifice may work.

name: Space advantage
mnemonic: More space, more room to manoeuvre — but more ground to defend.
summary: Pawns further up the board give your pieces more squares behind them and restrict the opponent's pieces.
points: White's pawns on c4, d5 and e4 claim the queenside and centre; Black claims the kingside with ...f5.
The side with less space should trade pieces — cramped positions suffocate when crowded.
The side with more space should avoid trades and prepare a pawn break to open lines.

name: Good vs bad bishop
mnemonic: A bishop is bad when its own pawns stand on its colour.
summary: A bishop that is blocked by its own pawns is 'bad'; one whose pawns are on the other colour is 'good'.
points: Black's pawns on d5 and e6 sit on light squares, so the c8-bishop is hemmed in — a classic French bad bishop.
White's f1-bishop is good: his pawns on d4 and e5 are on dark squares, leaving its diagonals open.
Plans: trade your bad bishop (...b6 and ...Ba6), or put your pawns on the other colour.

name: Initiative
mnemonic: Make threats; force your opponent to react instead of plan.
summary: The player who makes the threats dictates the game. The initiative can be worth a pawn or more.
points: Black is a pawn down, but every move came with a threat: ...Na5 hit the bishop, ...h6 the knight, ...e4 the knight again.
While White retreats, Black develops; soon ...Bc5/...Bd6, ...O-O and ...Qc7 follow with an attack.
To keep the initiative, keep creating threats — one quiet move can hand it back.
